title: How do expressions change along the paths of the figure?
description: In the figure, ovals hold expressions and boxes hold operations. One path turns w plus two into four w plus twenty, and the video fills the blanks on three more paths by carrying out each operation on the expression.
teaching_notes: One idea: each box changes the expression in the oval before it, and a multiplying box multiplies every term. Watch for students who multiply only the letter and leave the number unchanged.

video_script.why: A learner uses the method of the bracket: a number that multiplies an expression multiplies every term inside it, and like terms are joined.
video_script.substitution: The method of opening a bracket such as two times the bracket y minus one, with three times the bracket w minus three.
video_script.anchor: a figure of ovals that hold expressions and boxes that hold operations, joined by paths
video_script.payoff_line: Every blank oval now holds its expression

final_answer.spoken: three w minus nine, then w minus six and w minus ten, then w minus two and three w minus six

hold_back: Answer: 3w − 9 ; w − 6 then w − 10 ; w − 2 then 3w − 6
never_show: the missing expressions before the answer beat
maths_rules: given path: w + 2, add 3 gives w + 5, multiply by 4 gives 4w + 20
w + 2, subtract 8 gives w - 6, subtract 4 gives w - 10
w + 2, subtract 4 gives w - 2, multiply by 3 gives 3w - 6
video_script.design: One idea: each box acts on the expression in the oval before it, one box at a time. Assumes the example of opening a bracket. The given path is read first, then the blanks are filled on the stage.
open_questions: The figure is not in the extracted book text, so the paths and boxes follow the worklist steps and cannot be matched to the picture.

narration: <bookmark mark='gv1'/>Given, on one path w plus two goes through add three, and then multiply by four.
<bookmark mark='gv2'/>That makes w plus five. Then four times the bracket w plus five gives four w plus twenty.

narration: <bookmark mark='fd'/>We fill the blank ovals. We work the same way as the example in your book, opening each bracket.

marks.s1a: w − 3 enters the box multiply by 3

narration: <bookmark mark='s1a'/>First, take w minus three and multiply it by three.
<bookmark mark='s1b'/>Three multiplies both terms, so three times w is three w, and three times three is nine. The oval holds three w minus nine.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: w + 2, subtract 8: w + 2 − 8 = w − 6 ; subtract 4: w − 6 − 4 = w − 10

marks.s2a: w + 2 enters the box subtract 8 and w − 6 is written
marks.s2b: w − 6 enters the box subtract 4 and w − 10 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='s2a'/>Second, take w plus two and subtract eight. Two minus eight is minus six, so the oval holds w minus six.
<bookmark mark='s2b'/>Then subtract four from that. Minus six minus four is minus ten, so the next oval holds w minus ten.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: w + 2, subtract 4: w + 2 − 4 = w − 2 ; multiply by 3: 3 × (w − 2) = 3w − 6

marks.s3a: w + 2 enters the box subtract 4 and w − 2 is written
marks.s3b: w − 2 enters the box multiply by 3 and 3w − 6 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='s3a'/>Third, take w plus two and subtract four. Two minus four is minus two, so the oval holds w minus two.
<bookmark mark='s3b'/>Then multiply by three. Three times w is three w, and three times minus two is minus six. The next oval holds three w minus six.

beats.on_screen: Step 4, check with w = 10: 3 × 7 = 21 = 3w − 9 ; 4 and 0 for w − 6 and w − 10 ; 8 and 24 for w − 2 and 3w − 6

narration: <bookmark mark='s4a'/>Fourth, check with w as ten. Three times seven is twenty one, and three w minus nine is also twenty one.
<bookmark mark='s4b'/>Twelve minus eight is four, and four minus four is zero. Twelve minus four is eight, and three times eight is twenty four.
